Corrupt Electoral Practices
On the orders of the day:

I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) during his speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne raised a grave issue-

What is the question?
Mr. SPEAKER. Order. I must ask the hon. member to put his question immediately if he has one to direct to the government.

My question is: Is it the intention of the government to have the matter raised by the leader of the opposition concerning corrupt electoral practices referred to the committee on privileges and elections under standing order No. 63, or referred to some other committee of this house for investigation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) informed me before the house opened of his intention to ask a question with respect to corrupt election practices. As he apparently is not familiar with the law on the subject or the rules of the house with regard to procedure in such matters I have drafted a statement which I shall give in reply to his question.
Parliament has made statutory provision for the investigation of corrupt practices at elections. Under the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, chapter 50, Revised Statutes of. Canada, 1927, any person who has the right to vote may present a petition to a judge of a supreme or superior court, setting out these practices, and, if a deposit of SI,000 is made, an investigation may be held. Under the Corrupt Practices Inquiries Act, chapter 51, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, twenty-five or more electors may present a petition to the House of Commons charging the existence of such practices, and, if a deposit of $1,000 is made, the house may direct the government to appoint a commission for the purpose of making an inquiry. The commission in either case must submit a report to parliament, and under standing order No. 79 it is provided that if it appears that any person has been elected by corrupt practices the house will proceed with the utmost severity.
Since parliament passed the above legislation the committee on privileges and elections has never held any investigation with respect to the election of members. In the present instance no specific charges have been made
and no petition has been presented to the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I think the statement that the committee on privileges and elections has never held an investigation is not correct; in the case of Huron North there was an investigation.

Will the government take up with the government of the United States and the governments of Ontario and New York state the question of erecting joint regulation works in this river to prevent the recurrence of the abnormal conditions which have recently arisen?
In reply I may say that the situation arising from the recent ice jam is such an extremely unusual one, even for the Niagara river, that the possibility and warranty of effecting any measures to prevent or mitigate a recurrence would require careful study on the part of the interests which have been adversely affected. Regulation works which were proposed by the international board of engineers at the outlet of the Niagara river in connection with the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence seaway scheme would not appear to be of any benefit to a situation such as has now arisen.
The second question was:
Has the minister any ice-breaking plants for use on lake Erie and the Niagara river

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. N. Francceur for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Bennett.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the speech from the throne the government take a great deal of credit for improved economic conditions throughout the country. They point to mounting revenues and increased export trade. I should like to ask in what fields these increased revenues and export trade lie. They arise largely, I submit, through the exploitation of Canada's mineral wealth, often by foreign corporations. What accounts for the demand for these minerals? I submit again that it is war in the far east and in Europe and the vast rearmament programs that are seen everywhere throughout the world. Indiscriminately at the present time we sell to both aggressor and victim, although I might add that often only the aggressor can obtain the supplies that he needs. We refuse to supply a legitimate government in Spain with men and goods, yet we are exporting large quantities of goods to Japan for use against China. Our export figures to-day represent, in part, the price that is being paid by the mangled bodies of women and children in congested Chinese cities, and I say further that prosperity based upon such factors is deceptive and will not last. It is disease, not health, that enriches Canada, and wealth thus gained must bring its own nemesis eventually.
A Liberalism which boasts of such trade is not the Liberalism of Gladstone, who in a previous century thundered against the atrocities in Armenia and elsewhere. During Christmas time I saw a cartoon which illustrates what I mean. It showed a picture of Santa Claus, labelled Canada; below there was a country labelled China. Santa Claus was riding in a Japanese plane, showering Christmas gifts-bombs made in part from materials obtained from Canada-upon the Chinese. So I say that a government which boasts of such trade returns and at the same time allows present conditions to exist in the great stricken areas of western Canada without doing something effective to meet those conditions, should not boast.

I should like .to say something about conditions in the province from which I come. Men and women there have sown for years and have failed to reap. We know that. After recent trips over the prairie provinces I would say that conditions there are reaching the point where many of our people are in a state of despair. From year to year we have drifted along with relief costs mounting and nothing done on a wide scale to meet the situation. On another occasion, when a resolution standing on the order paper in my name proposing a comprehensive inquiry into the possibility of widespread irrigation and water conservation projects is before us, I want to go into that question rather more fully. It is sufficient to say now that I have been all over the area more than once this year and have been greatly depressed by what I have seen there.
Much more was I depressed last year to see that the government were not taking effective steps early enough-and may I emphasize those words "early enough"-to meet the situation that was upon us last summer. At the end of June in the town of Rosetown, in my own constituency, I addressed a meeting of farmers and business people at which resolutions were passed urging the government to take immediate and effective steps to retain in its present position the grain that was then in the elevators in that constituency, in order to protect the people of that area. A week later I attended a meeting of over a thousand farmers in the town of Perdue. I may say that it was not a partisan meeting. I did not know it was being called. I was invited to it, as were also the former Conservative member for the constituency and the Liberal candidate in the last election. There again resolutions were passed pointing out the situation and emphasizing the need for the conservation of the seed and feed then in that area. Those resolutions were forwarded to Ottawa, yet my observation was that in the weeks that followed the elevators were virtually emptied of the grain that was there.
I know I shall be told that one reason was that the cash price of wheat at that particular time was higher than the futures price and that the elevators could not be expected to retain that grain against future need. On the part of the elevator companies I say that was perfectly natural. I say further, however, that the government, if it had wished, could have closed the speculative market; it could have discontinued the trading in futures and indemnified the companies involved, if necessary, against subsequent loss due to that

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
governmental action. But it allowed that speculative market, about which I have complained from time to time, to continue to operate. The government, which had destroyed the effectiveness of the wheat board method of marketing, again remained inert in the face of the impending crisis. Can we wonder if the farmers believe the statement that the party now in office at least to some extent was a beneficiary in connection with campaign funds from members of the grain trade? That is a suggestion which is made from time to time. The other evening in the house we heard a more specific statement by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and, later, briefly mentioning the matter in his speech, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that he would like advice as to how the situation could be dealt with.
The time has come, in the interests of clean and decent government in Canada, when political parties should be compelled to publish the sources of all their campaign funds-all of them-in order that we may know the interests and influences behind the election of governments in this country. In any event the two things the farmers believe the grain trade desired have been accomplished, namely the virtual abandonment of the wheat board method of marketing, and the subsequent sale to grain brokers, on the speculative exchange, of the grain held.
The result of the condition to which I have referred means that the government has had to ship in grain for feed and, in the spring, will have to ship in grain for seed. This means that farmers unfortunate enough to have neither seed nor feed, or only one or the other, will be penalized both ways on that account. Then, had the government had the board in operation, it could have relieved the situation for the man who had a little crop to sell. Only yesterday I received a letter from a constituent at McGee, in my constituency, in which he complains to me that when grain is delivered in a wagonload lot farmers have to take the future, not the cash price. I believe I understand why that is so. Nevertheless, because of the unusual situation in connection with cash and future market prices, it means a loss of from twenty to thirty cents a bushel for those men who are delivering small quantities of grain at various times. Delivery to the wheat board could have protected these men who have a little grain to sell in a year when every cent counts.
Further, in June, July and even in August the government did not act quickly enough in regard to the matter of feed fodder. They failed to secure the necessary feed, and the result is that to-day herds of cattle and horses
have been disposed of or destroyed. Undoubtedly some will starve on our western plains this winter. So that the whole of our live stock industry in many parts of Saskatchewan, consisting of herds founded with a great deal of difficulty, expense and care, will be destroyed. The very basis of that part of our economic life will at least to some extent be destroyed.
Yet there was feed. I am told that hay remained uncut in Manitoba. I did not see it; but as I travelled through Manitoba during the first week in September, across the Portage plains where nature had been bountiful, I did see no less than fourteen large straw stacks burning at one time.

speechtext: I wrote the Minister of Agriculture about it, and his reply now is that it had sow thistle in it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I saw it on the same day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I know there is some sow thistle on the Portage plains, but, too, I have seen hay which had sow thistle in it, shipped from the northern to the southern part of my province. Of course, if the reason stated by the minister is the correct one it puts another complexion upon the story. I do know, however, that the government did not act quickly enough in obtaining the necessary straw and in providing the men and equipment to bale and ship it.
I have spoken about the cattle. Of the poverty, misery, despair and want in many Saskatchewan homes I do not wish to say much to-day. Later in the session there will be opportunity for such discussion. May I say just in passing that those of us interested in the condition of the Saskatchewan people are grateful for the efforts of the people in the other provinces who sent into Saskatchewan large quantities of foodstuffs for distribution through a voluntary committee. But when I hear boasting from the govem-[DOT] ment side about prosperity I think of those people on the prairie, and I realize that after all the boasting is pretty hollow.
May I repeat what I have said before, that the condition is not entirely due to drought. The brief on behalf of Saskatchewan filed only a few days ago before the Rowell commission clearly proves my point. I know that when both in and out of the house I have made that statement on previous occasions, it has been questioned. But in the presentation of an excellent brief the government of Saskatchewan has shown that, as is so often said, one or two good crops will not rehabilitate the condition of the people in that province.
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

The drought was but the last of a long series of economic disasters, including a long period of low prices when at times our farmers obtained only twenty cents a bushel for No. 1 wheat delivered at local elevators.
I would add that upon the rehabilitation of this region in no small measure depends the entire economic structure of Canada. In a country such as ours we cannot reduce hundreds of thousands of people to peasantry, and at the same time have the great industries in eastern Canada, and the great transportation systems, in a prosperous condition. That simply cannot be done. Yet there are those who would advise us to resign ourselves to a low standard of living and the virtual peasantry to which I have just referred.
For example, I notice that the report of a speech by the Minister of Agriculture before a group of prominent Quebec Liberals at the Reform club in Montreal on January 17, appears in the Montreal Gazette in these words:
There were one million people living in the drought affected areas, said Mr. Gardiner. Were they to be moved ? He did not think so, but they would have to become accustomed to conditions. After all there was nothing specially new in the western situation. Farmers many years ago had been "on relief." His own grandfather in Huron county, Ontario, had received governmental assistance.
If we accept that philosophy, we are in effect accepting a philosophy of despair. Our grandfathers were in poverty, our fathers were in poverty and, 'therefore, we must get used to the poverty with which we are surrounded. That is the interpretation I would place upon those words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is not the correct one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to have the minister correct it when I am finished. That is the philosophy which is being put forth in certain parts of Canada. I regret very much that this statement should have been made in 'eastern Canada, in the city of Montreal. I have had an opportunity of speaking there and I know that many people in that city do not appreciate or understand our western situation.
I believe that much can be done to improve -the condition of agriculture. We could plan our production more wisely and guarantee a better standard of living to our farmers and to the great masses of people in the cities. From time to time we in this comer will be glad to contribute any ideas that we may have which may tend to bring about those improved standards.
If we got to work and grappled with the situation we would be able to find a solution
[Mr. Coldwall.J
for many of our economic and social difficulties. As our leader (Mr. Woodsworth) said yesterday, I believe that prosperity in this country is spotty, unsound and insecure. Because I believe that, I am going to support the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I intend to take that action because I believe the present government is engaged in what amounts to a policy of social and economic drifting. To drift is to court disaster and endanger the foundations of our democratic institutions'.
Let us not forget that everywhere democracy is being attacked. A few years ago we might have said with Sinclair Lewis, "It Can't Happen Here," but today we know that it is being said by many that our democratic institutions are inefficient and unsatisfactory. The drifting of this parliament in the last two years lends colour to that accusation. When unemployment is rampant, when poverty and misery are widespread, when the legitimate aspirations of our young people are thwarted, then it would seem that the existing order, no matter what it may be, is threatened. I am in agreement with those who criticize this drift.
In common with the rest of the world we must move in the direction of a more equitable distribution of wealth. That would in my opinion ultimately involve the social ownership of the principal means of production and of our resources, but as a realist I know that at the moment possibly this and some other countries are not prepared to take a step of that kind. But there are other steps which could be taken and my criticism is that we are not taking those steps. Before the last election we heard hon. members who now sit on the government side say that national control of currency and credit must be utilized for the common good. Yet nothing has been done by this parliament although we in this comer have from time to time introduced resolutions dealing with this particular matter. There are steps we could take if we would, but we are doing nothing to alleviate the conditions with which we are surrounded.
If that alleviation is attempted we in this group are prepared to cooperate. Ever since I have been a member of the house I have appreciated that sitting around me on all sides were members who desired to do something for this country. Yet we do nothing. Again and again we talk in terms of our respective political parties when we ought to be talking and thinking in terms of this dominion and the citizens thereof. Because

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
year after year passes with parliament doing nothing people are lending ready ears to all kinds of subversive propaganda.
Who can say that a Canadian form of nazism is not raising its ugly head across the country? To refer again to the Montreal Gazette, that paper published recently a picture of Canadian nazis drilling under the direction of retired regular army officers. The inside pages contained photographs of the office of the organization with the swastika on the wall. There was also a photograph of the leader of the movement in the province of Quebec. We hear a great deal of the dangers of communistic propaganda, but to my mind Canada faces a grave danger to-day from nazi propaganda and the fascist forces which are being used by powerful interests. It is obvious that these organizations have large sums of money available for literature and uniforms. I shall not deal at any length with the padlock law in the province of Quebec, as that was gone into fully yesterday.
The same kind of thing can be found elsewhere in Canada. Looking back to last April we find the Liberal premier of Ontario saying to a group of people, " You shall not organize in the association of your choice." The institutions of this country are said to be British, and under British institutions we are said to be free to organize. Looking back into history I remember reading of an occurrence in 1834 near the place where I was bom. A group of agricultural labourers led by a local preacher, George Loveless, who was also a labourer, endeavoured to bring about some improvement in their lot. Six of them were arrested and cast into prison. They were tried and the judge in passing sentence used these words: "Not for anything that you have done nor, as I can prove, that you intended to do, do I sentence you to seven years' transportation across His Majesty's high seas." Not for anything you have done nor, as I can prove, for anything that you intend to do. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in effect those are the words that were used in this province last April in connection with an organization there.
But see what happened. History, may I remark, sometimes repeats itself. At that time, 103 or 104 years ago, the first Liberal government sat in power in England; to-day in Canada a Liberal government sits in power; and again, in effect, the same thing is being said in Ontario and Quebec-not for anything you have done nor, as I can prove, for anything you intend to do, do I stop you from doing these things. Yet out of that came one of the greatest social and economic movements that the world has ever seen-the
rise of the great British trades union movement, and the rise of the great cooperative movement. Democracy must be preserved, and if it is going to be preserved, these rights must be assured to our people, and pressing reforms must be made to alleviate their condition. Theories of many types we may hold, but the cry is for practical and immediate solutions of the problems that press the Canadian people at the present time. In the west the cry for an effective rehabilitation plan goes up, and may I say to my friends from constituencies in eastern Canada that no longer can the west be regarded as a sort of rich colonial possession to be exploited by other parts of Canada or by foreign lands, but if they will examine the matter they will find that that has been to a degree the history of the west. We have no secondary industries established there.
In connection with social reforms, the other day. the Prime Minister chided the leader of the opposition for his failure to enact constitutionally unemployment insurance and other social measures. I should like to remark that some of the difficulties that we are meeting today are because in those years when business was on an upswing, between 1921 and 1929, if you like to take the years of Liberal administration, social measures, and unemployment insurance in particular, formed planks in the Liberal platform, and yet none of these measures was enacted nor was any preparation made constitutionally to enact them.
Exploitation of the farmer and the worker everywhere has been carried on by industry and finance, and it must be stopped if our national unity and well-being are to be preserved. We saw what that exploitation was to some extent in the textile probe; we also had an illuminating inquiry into the high prices of agricultural implements, and one of the things I am anxious to know this session is what we are going to do about these matters. Are the two reports that were made on those subjects simply to be filed and be of record, and be forgotten, or is the government going to bring down legislation to deal effectively with the problems which those reports indicate do exist? If such action is forthcoming, the speech from the throne remains silent about it, and I must say that the inaction of the government in the past two years in the fields to which I have referred does not lead me to expect them to do very much. In fact, their record fills me with some misgiving.
There is, I know, a feeling of satisfaction on the government side of the house regarding

The Address-Mr. Caldwell
the recent by-elections, and I do not want to take away from hon. members opposite any of the glory they take to themselves from those results; but I will say this, that when ministers go into Montreal and say, "We will fill the hole on Dorchester street," when they say, in effect we will spend millions of dollars right alongside this constituency, or when their supporters go right across the country to British Columbia and say in Victoria, "It would be well at this time if this city were represented in the Liberal caucus because there are large defence appropriations to be considered,"-when these things are said, some at least of the glory of winning by-elections fades out of sight. The tragedy is that our Canadian electorate falls for that kind of campaigning.
But in spite of any victories the government may have won, there is grave unrest throughout this land, and that grave unrest is particularly apparent among our youth, who are denied the opportunities of life which we ourselves had when we were young. I meet a good many of them across the country, well equipped, but unable to find an outlet for their legitimate ambitions, their training and attainments. Thus far, I would say to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), our attempts to deal with that problem have been quite feeble. These young people cannot lead normal lives, cannot marry and settle down and make homes as we could do, and so the very fibre of our society is being destroyed; its very foundation, the home, is being undermined. People look to this parliament for a lead and for a solution, and if they are not given a lead and some hope of a solution, then democracy in this country will be in danger.
Last session parliament did very little because of the haste to bring the proceedings to a close in time for the coronation and the imperial conference. But this session is a challenge to us all. Surely there are enough members in the house who realize the situation-I know there are but very often party discipline prevents them from expressing themselves as they might otherwise do-who must wish to indicate their dissatisfaction, and I would say, let them do so by voting for the amendment rather than for the motion. In that way we can make our protest effective in the only manner in which protests by members of parliament can be made effective, and that is by our votes on the floor of the house. If a sufficient number did that, we might find ways and means of compelling the

government to consider taking effective steps; and, may I add, with the clouds of war and of recession or depression, whichever you like to call it, gathering in the distance, we dare not continue to drift along for another session. With the poverty and the misery, and the devastation even, that exists in large sections of this country, we must not let a false prosperity here and there deceive or blind us to the real issues.
I know, again, it will be pointed out that dividends have increased. Truly wealth is becoming accumulated; monopoly holds us ever in a firmer grip. On the other side, these piling dividends and wealth accumulations are paralleled by misery, by want, by despair, by the denial of opportunity, and all the rest of it. And we must, in this parliament, discover ways and means of increasing wealth for the great masses and of redistributing that wealth and purchasing power among the masses of the people. It seems to me that the problems before us fall under two heads: internal- thinking now of what the papers have published lately-and external peace; and, second, social security. These, it seems to me, cover the whole fields of foreign policy, rehabilitation, debt, purchasing power, housing, pensions for the aged, opportunity for youth, and the like; and parliament should not rise this session, even if we sit here for a whole year, until some solutions have been found. If the government fails, as it has so far failed, to formulate an effective policy, then let us, the members of the house, forget our party differences and our pet ideas-

speechtext:
Before I present to this august assembly the few remarks which I have prepared for this afternoon, I wish to protest against the extremely bad lighting arrangements we who sit in the fifth row enjoy here. I am very well


The Address-Mr. Mallette
acquainted with the fact that the hon. members who sit here, and I suppose the same can be said of those who sit opposite in the same row, are men of such talent that they will eventually move to the second or even to the front row, but those who succeed us will have the same trouble. My vision has declined a good deal since I came here. I do not want any of my hon. friends to go blind for lack of a slight expenditure which this country can well afford, and I do hope, sir, that you in your official capacity as presiding officer of this chamber will draw the attention of the powers that be to this very bad condition and have it remedied as soon as possible.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, you will have the kindness to allow me to add my very sincere congratulations to those that have already been offered to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both of these gentlemen have acquitted themselves with great credit and fully in accordance with the best traditions of this parliament. Both have delivered eloquent and patriotic speeches which were duly appreciated by hon. members and which proved the sagacity of those who selected them for the discharge of this important task. Other speeches, all very interesting, followed. Hon. members will forgive me if I do not refer to every one of them; I shall limit myself to a very short reference to the speech made by the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bennett), and the one made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). These two gentlemen occupy the highest places in Canadian public life, and what they say is always listened to with the greatest possible attention.
It was evident that the right hon. the leader of the opposition was not pleased with the speech from the throne. He found fault with it from beginning to end, with one sole exception, if I am not mistaken, and that exception was the reference to the coronation of their majesties. If this important event had not been referred to, the leader of the opposition apparently would have been willing to drop overboard the whole speech, lock, stock and barrel. Upon any stranger totally unacquainted with Canadian politics who might have been within hearing distance of the right hon. -gentleman the effect of such a clever attack would have been stupendous-that is, until that same stranger heard the reply of our revered leader, the Prime Minister. The leader of the opposition conjured up such a heavy smoke screen that the speech from the throne had become almost invisible behind it, but the Prime Minister in his eloquent reply completely disposed of
this smoke screen and rapidly chased it out of sight. This is most remarkable because the Prime Minister's reply apparently was based solely on notes which he took during the attack, while his worthy opponent must have had plenty of time to prepare his well planned assault.
An interesting revelation was made to this house by the right hon. gentleman who with such talent leads the opposition. Please see page 40 of Hansard and read what the right hon. gentleman has to say about the trade agreement with the United States. It is evident that -the government over which he presided-I am not quite sure that this is correct, but we will say, the government over which he presided-did discuss a trade agreement with the United States. And why should he not have discussed a trade agreement with our neighbours? It is not we of the Liberal party who will find fault with such a move. We have always favoured closer commercial relations with our southern neighbours of the great American republic. If the Tory party saw fit in the interests of Canada to borrow that plank of the Liberal party, well and good. But I could not help thinking, and surely other hon. members, and Canadians throughout the dominion, cannot help thinking that the Conservative party or its very able leader must have undergone a change of heart, because in the ears of those of my generation who cast their first vote at the general election of 1911 there still rings the battle cry of the Tory party in that election, a battle cry that rang throughout Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific-"No truck or trade with the Yankees!" I am glad to learn of that change of heart. Canada is on the American continent, c'est un pays d'Amerique, and we should have pleasant business relations with our neighbours to the south. Apparently the Conservative party shares our view of that part of the Liberal policy, and of course that makes it unanimous.
There is no doubt about the improvement in conditions generally. There is equally no doubt that we have not yet reached the goal which we are seeking, but we believe the Liberal party has the policy best suited to attain that result. Better trade relations with the rest of the world will permit us to dispose profitably of the production of Canadian farms and Canadian workmen. The efforts of the present government in -that direction are already bearing fruit, and the Canadian public notes with deep satisfaction that that same government is ever on the alert, constantly seeking ways and means of further improving conditions and of improving them for all. The Liberal policy is not designed for the specific benefit of any particular class,

The Address-Mr. Mallette
but has everyone in mind. The county of Jacques Cartier which I have the honour to represent has considerable farming area, and truck gardens and market gardens are numerous. There are also several important manufacturing establishments. It is in a small way a cross-section of Canada. If I am correctly informed, two-fifths of the population are of English descent, and therefore the county is bilingual. We all live happily together without friction concerning language or religion. Notwithstanding any political differences, my best efforts are directed to maintaining and improving this harmonious state of things.
We are glad to get a fair share of the benefits accruing to Canada, thanks to the wise administration of the present government. But, sir, material progress is not everything; it is not the sole thing to aim at. It is also necessary that peace and harmony reign in the country. It is indispensable that the different sections of Canada respect and esteem one another. It is essential that the rights of everyone be respected. In a word, all citizens of Canada should be good Canadians. That applies in public life as well as in private life. The ancestors of those of us who live in lower Canada entered confederation as partners, with all that word implies both as to obligations and privileges. No province in this confederation should be treated by the others as a poor relation; that would result in the destruction of our present national structure, and the beautiful dream of our forefathers of creating a great nation by the union of all the British territories lying north of the United States would be shattered forever. I repeat, our ancestors joined confederation as partners. And their descendants are willing, nay eager, to continue on that basis; only on such a basis of equity, justice and British fair play can confederation continue. Persons in positions of authority in either the national or provincial capitals who walk about with chips on their shoulders are not serving the cause of national unity. In politics one should be ready and willing to put water in his wine when occasion calls for it. Only in heeding and practising the words of the Master, "Peace on earth to men of good will," can Canada become a great nation.
Confederation became an accomplished fact through the acceptance of an act called the British North America Act. This act has been operative since July 1, 1867. It has been amended from time to time, chiefly I believe on account of territorial changes. At the present day there is a demand that it be

amended again, this time to give the dominion government the right to pass social legislation. It is quite possible that after seventy years the act may be in need of revision, although the average Canadian citizen must wonder as to the necessity for such revision. Be that as it may, the call for amendment has been strong enough to cause the federal government to resolve to investigate conditions. The government therefore appointed the Rowell commission, which is now at work touring the dominion to hear all and sundry who desire to offer suggestions, cures and panaceas for the correction of our economic and legislative ills, real and imaginary. Probably there will be another opportunity to speak on this subject later, so today I content myself with saying that the British North America Act should not be amended without the consent of all the participants to its creation; I mean all the provinces. No one in this parliament, I am sure, wants to impose anything upon the provinces; no one wants to violate provincial rights; no political party to my knowledge has any such plank in its platform. On the contrary, all hon. members of this house are very respectful of such rights. But after seventy years it is within the realm of possibility that improvements are desirable in that act-I prefer the word "improvements" to the word "amendments." Those who want unemployment insurance are citizens of their respective provinces, as well as of the dominion. No one can be a Canadian without being at the same time a citizen of one of the provinces. As a Canadian an individual is perhaps enabled to take a broader view of things in general than he would get from a purely provincial point of view, just as the man who has seldom left the locality in which he was bom gets a broader conception of things when he travels and visits other communities.
It is, I hope, unnecessary for me to state that I use the word "provincial" in no disparaging sense whatsoever. A lot of trouble would be avoided if we knew one another better within the boundaries of our well beloved country. And as it is generally Quebec that is considered different I think that occasion should be taken by those of our fellow citizens who live in other provinces to visit Quebec and get better acquainted; and the reverse should also take place, that those who live in Quebec should arrange to visit other parts of the country. Some universities in the great province of Ontario have already made a good move in that direction, by holding summer schools at different points in Quebec. This idea of citizens visiting different parts

The Address-Mr. Mallette
of their country is not a new one. Years ago I saw that Signor Mussolini had arranged to give free wedding trips to Rome to newly married couples. However, I am not suggesting that we should go that far yet.
The leader of the opposition spoke the other day of political corruption. I sincerely hope his party is with him in his opposition to political corruption, because again that would make it unanimous, because we have always been against corruption from the start. I hope the right hon. gentleman will transmit that conviction to his party managers in the county I have the honour to represent-they are badly in need of it.
May I state that there are different forms of corruption. One form is gerrymandering, and that has been practised by hon. gentlemen on my left with an art deserving of a better cause. They are past masters at it.

speechtext: That is old; we have had that before.

speechtext:
Well, it has to be repeated so as to sink in, and I hope it will sink into the mind of the hon. member. If the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) is willing to correct it, I hope he will get the ear of his revered leader and ask him to support me in my efforts to change the boundaries of the county of Jacques Cartier to more nearly where they ought to be and would be if common sense had been the guide when the redistribution was made in 1931. My hon. friends are experts at that game. I know it is not new; the hon. member is very kind in reminding me of that. I remember reading about it years ago in the Remin-iseenses of Sir Richard Cartwright, who was no young chicken, and he said that in those days they did not call it gerrymandering, but "hiving the Grits." As far as Quebec is concerned, they are not hiving the Grits but hiving the Tories. But in hiving the Tories injustice is sometimes done. I have no objection to Quebec having some Tory members; it is a good thing, but I hope that in future redistributions common sense will prevail, as I am sorry to say it did not prevail in the last redistribution. If the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition wants to know about the corrupt practices of his organizers I have a suggestion to make to him. It is simply this, that one of these evenings when the house is not in session he call together in his office or in his rooms at the Chateau- or over in Hull-a caucus of Liberal members. Every one of us will be able to give him some very illuminating stories of the way some of the Tory organizers go about 51952-8
it. I dare say the right hon. gentleman is not acquainted with such things personally, because usually it is good practice for those leading political parties not to have such knowledge, but when the word "corruption" is brought up we have to get down to the bottom of the matter, and I hope, my suggestion will be followed.
In Quebec the clergy have been making a splendid fight against electoral corruption, but in my opinion corruption should be dealt with at other times as well as during elections. I think a start should be made in our churches, universities and schools. Of course it would take a generation or more to educate the people, but it would be well worth while, because after all such things as dishing out whisky to right and left at election time, so that in the end nobody gains anything, should be stopped, and the sooner that is done the better for the respectability of elections and the respectability of politics in Canada. I am quite willing to do my share, as far as that goes.
If I am not mistaken, Mr. Speaker, some hon. member has raised an objection to the construction of a subway under the Lachine canal, which was very much discussed in the by-election in St. Henry on January 17, which resulted in another remarkable victory for the government now in office. It is easy to understand why that subway played such a prominent part in that by-election. The division of St. Henry is in the southwestern section of Montreal. It is cut almost in half by the Lachine canal. It is not the fault of the people who live south of the canal that the canal was constructed; it was the fault of the Lachine rapids and the canal was built because it is impossible for ships to pass through the rapids westward. The people living south of that canal have a great deal of trouble at times to cross over. They have a bridge at Cote St, Paul, a bridge about a mile away at Yille St. Pierre and a bridge about a half or three-quarters of a mile below at Atwater avenue, so it is only natural that the people in that section want a subway to be constructed under that canal. The canal is a federal undertaking, built, I presume, by the federal government or by its predecessor before confederation, and the people living in that district are simply the victims. It seems to me that we might better have spent our money in building that subway instead of giving it out in doles. This is a chance to correct that mistake. I mentioned that matter myself during the by-election, and I sincerely hope that work will be undertaken. This is no new suggestion. The former



The Address-Mr. Mallette
member for that constituency, Mr. Mercier, worked very hard in that connection also.
Reference has been made as well to the Canadian National terminal in Montreal. Well, that terminal was part of a scheme for the improvement of railway conditions in Montreal, begun by Sir Henry Thornton, involving a good many changes in the location of the tracks and the erection of a station worthy of the metropolis of Canada. Immediately after the election in 1930 work was stopped, we were informed under instructions from Ottawa. I hope the gentlemen who know all the facts in this connection some day will come out in the open and explain exactly what happened and why it happened. If that is done the political fortunes of some people in Montreal will suffer a good deal, but truth will be served. So I hope that some day either in this house or outside of it-it does not matter so long as we are told-we may hear exactly what happened at that time.
My views in connection with that station are simply these: Bonaventure station in Montreal is a sight. You know, the word "sight" may have two or three meanings, and in this case you may take the worst. The Canadian National, in addition to showing a deficit, is of some use to this country, and it should have a decent terminal in Montreal. I believe this matter should be looked at from the point of view of the interests of Canada rather than the selfish interests of Montreal or my constituency. There should be a station at Montreal adequate to take care of the needs of the travelling public. In December, 1936, just before the municipal elections in Montreal, a strong delegation from that city came to Ottawa and interviewed the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), if I am not mistaken. I was present, together with nearly all the members from the district of Montreal. I gave my views then, but I do not mind giving them again. I believe that station should be built, and moreover I believe it should be built for the Canadian people, not merely for the Canadian National Railways. I may shock some people both here and outside the august precincts of this house, but I believe the Canadian Pacific should have access to that terminal also. The Canadian Pacific is a very large contributor to the upbuilding of this country, and it should be so arranged that a traveller coming to Montreal by way of the Canadian Pacific and wishing to transfer to the Canadian National should be able to do so at the one station.

I believe also, Mr. Speaker, that the terminal should be within easy reach of the harbour and the aviation field. I am sorry that the Montreal airport is so far from the centre of the city. I know it was built by a Liberal administration, but I do not know why it was placed so far away when there are many suitable locations much closer at hand and much more convenient to the travelling public. I was of the opinion that the terminal should be made available also to the automobile bus lines that make Montreal their headquarters, but unfortunately that is impossible now because the Colonial Coach Lines and the Provincial Transport at last are erecting their own terminal opposite the Windsor hotel. We should not let any more opportunities of this kind escape us. Let us go ahead with this work, which is not antagonistic to anybody but is simply in the interests of Canada as a whole. In my humble opinion it is far better to give work to the people of Montreal than to give them the dole.
Yesterday the hon. gentleman who represents Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) presented his views in regard to a famous law in the province of Quebec known as the padlock law. I hold no brief for the government of Quebec; I do not believe they would trust me with a brief anyway, but I will say that it is quite possible that this law is capable of being amended, since it was passed in a hurry and may not be drafted quite properly. At the same time it represents, in a raw way, the point of view of the population of Quebec. Our people do not want communism. They will not have communism. They will fight communism. We believe in democracy; we are satisfied with Liberalism and Conservatism. There are some people who are talking about reorganizing the province along corporative lines, but most of us do not know much about that doctrine, and we are not scared. The matter is being studied by people who know what they are talking about, and when the time comes they will let us know the result of their studies.
The question of repealing the padlock law should be left to the people of Quebec; this government should not exercise its power of disallowance. If a demand comes from a strong section of the people of Quebec then the matter might be considered. However, one of these days the people of Quebec will have an opportunity to say at the polls whether or not they are satisfied with the government that passed that law, and it will be time enough to deal with the matter then. That is my point of view in that connection.

The Address-Mr. Mallette
In connection with our views on communism I want to quote from Le Devoir of November 2, 1937. This is an extract from an address given by His Eminence the Cardinal Archbishop of Quebec, speaking at the coliseum in Quebec city. The extract is as follows:
(Translation)
Freedom of speech
Under the mask of freedom of speech we are asked to listen to the most perverse doctors: Sophism and Hypocrisy. Freedom of speech, yes, but not freedom to outrage our social conceptions to insult our traditions, our principles and our religion.
Freedom of speech? Yes. indeed, but as it is practised among honourable people and not among imbeciles or brigands.
Freedom of speech! Are you in favour of freedom of the air? But do you extend that freedom to foreign appliances of war or strategical observation? Do you permit the plague-stricken, the germ-carriers to pollute, under pretext of equality, the pure air that surrounds us? Liberty, quite, but does liberty mean folly, connivance, unbridled licence?
We know very well that in a country like Canada, with such a sparse population, there are many things still to be accomplished. One of them is the abolition of slums in the large cities. The problem may not be a federal one, but sooner or later it may have to be linked up somehow with the Dominion Housing Act. By way of loans the dominion government helps to build houses; it also helps to repair them. Some day it may be called upon to help in some way towards the elimination of slums, and their replacement by decent buildings. In a country such as ours, one of such stupendous size, one in which there is so much unoccupied land, I believe every family should own its own home, and that our legislation should tend in that direction. A better distribution of wealth would do away with communism, and most of the other evils.
The employment commission has finished its work. May I say at this time that in my opinion it did good work, and it is to be hoped that some other agency will continue the good work which has been begun. I am pleased to be in a position to pay my tribute publicly to the men and women connected with the employment commission. In the constituency I have the honour to represent two of the schools for youth have been opened, one at Ste. Genevieve and the other at Macdonald college. We realize that this is just a trial but it is our sincere hope that great good will be the result. Those schools are operated under the Rogers-Bilodeau arrangement, and we hope that they will prove of the greatest possible benefit.
It is remarkable that the establishment of those schools coincides with the recommendations made by the Jeunesse Ouvriere Catholique, all of which can be read in a book entitled Un Moteur et des Ailes, which was written by M. Emile Benoist, at one time a member of the press gallery.
We have been subjected to propaganda from many sources in favour of immigration. I am thankful that in the speech from the throne there is no reference to any immigration program. It seems to me that the time is not yet ripe for it.
The last year and the present year mark the centenary of an important historical event in Canada, namely the rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada. There may be some difference of opinion as to whether or not the men who took up arms should have done so. I for one am convinced that if they were alive today they could have settled a similar dispute without resort to arms. Unfortunately they chose to do otherwise. However, whether or not we share the opinions they held as to the advisability or otherwise of resorting to arms, I think there can be only one stand we can take with respect to men who have been willing to die for their political opinions. Some died and some were hanged. That is the way political offenders were punished in those days.
About this time of the year one hundred years ago my own grandfather was in gaol as a rebel. He was a rebel because he believed in representative institutions for this country. Like many others, he was fighting to obtain what we now enjoy and what we are now trying to retain. The fact that that old gentleman was put in gaol as a rebel because he held those views is something of which I am very proud. I am sorry it has been left to me to be the first to mention the matter in parliament; in my opinion it should have come from higher quarters. But I do not want the descendants of those men who lived in Upper and Lower Canada to think that the heroes of 1837 and 1838 are the forgotten men of 1937 and 1938.
Now, a word as to armaments. The results in by-elections since the session of 1937 have been interpreted, in many quarters, as an unqualified endorsation of the program of this government with respect to national defence. Undoubtedly the electorate has expressed its confidence in the King administration. But please do not think that expenditures for armaments are, of themselves, the first and foremost cause of the popularity of the government. Do not jump to that conclusion. Undoubtedly the people of Canada will con-

The Address-Mr. Mallette
sent to sacrifices required for the defence of their national soil. The guarantees given by the Prime Minister and his colleagues during the last session, and given again by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in Lot-biniere and by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) in St. Henry that these expenditures are to be made solely for Canadian defence, have been accepted, because our citizens do not wish to be at the mercy of a coup de main by international hoodlums. But they have been accepted solely on the ground that they are expenditures for the protection of Canadian interests in Canada. Let us make that very clear. There is no desire, as I said before, to join any expedition to acquire oil wells or minerals which may be found elsewhere, in territories which are not British Let us understand that.
Before taking my seat I wish to speak with respect to the budget. The people of Canada are hoping for a balanced national budget. While I am not attempting to give advice to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who I see smiling in his seat, I shall take this opportunity to place upon Hansard a quotation from one of the works of one of the best known authors. I do so because I believe the quotation, at least to a certain extent, deals with budgets. In the session of 1936 we were given quotations from Carlyle almost every day. In that session Carlyle was certainly the popular author; he was quoted right and left, every day. There were no such quotations in 1937. I shall not quote Carlyle, because I believe the quoting of Carlyle in this chamber should be left entirely to the intelligentsia who ornament the front seats on both sides of this house.
I shall quote from another author whose works are well known not only where English is spoken, but where it is read. We know there are many people who can read a language but who cannot speak it. In plain language this author has been a man of the masses, a man of the people. Had he been in Canada, undoubtedly he would have been a Liberal. The house will understand, of course, that I refer to the well beloved Charles Dickens, and I read a quotation from David Copperfield for the consideration of the house and the special consideration of the Minister of Finance.
