speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate my neighbour, the hon. member who sits beside me (Mr. Mallette) upon his remarks and reiterate what he said with regard to the lighting in this part of the chamber. I thank him for the kind remarks he has made about the fifth row. I have no doubt that he was referring to this part of the chamber when he made mention of the intelligentsia. I should like also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the motion for and address in reply to the speech from the throne upon the manner in which they have conducted themselves. They have shown themselves worthy of the honour conferred upon them.
It has been gratifying to note that a further recovery has taken place during the past year in the trade of Canada. However, this increased trade does not seem to have brought about an appreciable improvement in the standard of living of our people. Improved conditions were noticeable up to October of last year, but they did not continue for the last three months of the year. Evidently we are following in the footsteps of the United States. If that country cannot stop itself going into a business tailspin, I hope we in Canada will be able to do so.
There is no doubt that the depression in the United States caused the dumping of a great deal of surplus stock into Canada at Christmas time. There has been an increase of SI 12,000 in the imports into Toronto alone for the month of January this year. Increased imports have affected our domestic production by way of diminished sales. The speech from the throne states that there will be an extension and revision of the trade agreement with the United States. I think any further concessions that it is contemplated we should give, should be very carefully considered by the government, in view of the fact that the unemployment situation in the United States is much worse than it is in Canada, they having some 10,000,000 workers unemployed at the present time. We must also remember that the average rate of duty on all imports into Canada in 1937 was only 13-7

The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
per cent. The average rate of duty on imports into the United States was 60 per cent. Even with the full reduction of 50 per cent which they are permitted to make, the average rate of duty would still be 30 per cent or 16 per cent higher than ours.
The population of my riding of St. Paul's is made up to a large extent of the finest type of industrial worker. They are dependent upon industry for their livelihood. At the present time considerable apprehension exists as to what action will be taken in respect to the lowering of our tariffs. This feeling of insecurity and uncertainty has had an adverse effect on business generally. If the government contemplates lowering tariffs it seems to me that it is only fair that the men in charge of our industries and the workers should be so advised and consulted. If not, they should have such knowledge. The heads of industries with extensive capital investment and payrolls of millions of dollars find themselves without knowledge of the negotiations with which to prepare a case for their industry against further tariff concessions to any outside country.	*
One class of industry in which some of my constituents are employed has a payroll of $25,000,000. A manufacturer of this class on which so many of my constituents depend for a livelihood has a well managed concern and pays highest wages. A reduction in the tariff might jeopardize this industry and the livelihood of many of my constituents. If there was a cessation or reduction in wages the wives and families of these workers would be seriously affected. This industry purchased 82,000,000 worth of raw materials from Australia and $3,000,000 worth from New Zealand. These purchases constituted 24 per cent of Canada's purchases from Australia and 58 per cent of the purchases from New Zealand. In addition this industry purchased manufactured products from other industries in Canada to the extent of many millions of dollars. Surely the heads of such an industry should have some intimation as to what is to be done with respect to tariffs. Profits have been too small to absorb the additional costs, due to a decreased output which would follow a tariff reduction.
The desire of labour is security based on a steady annual wage and continuous employment. A basis of factory production calculated to eliminate unsteady employment must of necessity be founded upon confidence in tariffs remaining established for a reasonable length of time. There are other classes of industries throughout the country, upon the continuous operation of which the industrial workers
depend for their living, they and their wives and families. It is only through continuous employment that a higher standard of living can be obtained-and it must be obtained. There should be more cooperation between governments and industry and business in general. This is absolutely necessary at least for the sake of the workers.
No mention has been made in the speech from the throne of any social legislation other than that with regard to unemployment insurance. When we consider the consequences, both economic and humanitarian, with respect to slums and the lack of low cost housing, as borne out by facts, and the experience of countries of the older lands in this respect,, we can understand it only as the laissez-faire-policy of the government. What is to become of those unfortunates who through n<3 fault of their own cannot earn enough with which to pay the rent of a decent home?
What about social legislation? The great social service of preventive medicine is functioning to try to keep them healthy and has kept thousands living, but no effort is indicated on the part of the government to help them, now that they are living, to make themselves happy and good citizens.
Something must be done. It is no wonder that we have communism and -many other "isms" in this country. The stability of a country arises out of the home. Our people must be made home-minded so that their children may be given the opportunity of becoming good Canadian citizens. I intend to say a word or two on this matter later on. I intend to do all I can to eliminate the conditions which one sees to-day.
On November 15, 1937, an order in council was passed making the outport of West Toronto a port. This order was to become effective on January 1, 1938. Up to the time of the passing of this order in council no public body or organization in the city of Toronto, so far as I know, had been consulted. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) thought that this radical change was of so little importance to the city of Toronto as to be not worth bothering much about.
I do not wish to decry the immediate estimated saving of some ten or twenty thousand dollars by the elimination of duplicate reporting or the like, for I think that is meritorious. But in passing I would ask, will there be a saving, when one considers the perquisites of a growing baby? And how, babies growl Are two head offices cheaper to maintain than a head office and a branch? I do not see how that is possible. I do not wish to discuss now the merits or demerits of
118	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Ross (St. Paul's)
the case, but a principle is involved. The board of trade of Toronto had knowledge of the order in council some time after November 15, and they wrote the minister on December 3, setting out their case. The minister's reply was dated December 8.
The board again wrote on December 23, setting forth further arguments and requesting that until certain information in reply to questions asked of the minister had been made known to the public, the matter be left in abeyance. I shall take the opportunity at some future date of reading these questions. The minister replied on December 30. refusing that request. The board of control also wired the minister on December 29, making a similar request.
There are organizations of public-spirited citizens in Toronto, such as the mayor and board of control, the board of trade, and the Toronto industrial commission, who are only too glad to give the benefit of their counsel when asked. There are also members of parliament representing the city of Toronto.
The request made by the city council and the board of trade was, I think, a reasonable one, and it should not have been cast aside as of no value. I think they have a better opportunity to appreciate the effect of such a change as this. That is their job. I think that a city of the size and importance of Toronto has a right to more consideration, cooperation and confidence in a matter of such import.
Now a word about broadcasting. Is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation making itself an agency for encouraging the very thing which it was created to discourage, that is, the extension of radio advertising, and particularly of advertising which does not originate in Canada? To encourage such advertising has an adverse effect upon Canadian enterprise through making the corporation's facilities available to American advertisers at rates which a commercial enterprise could not begin to consider. If this is so, it seems to be a serious misuse of public revenues and credit.
Does not the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation take an entirely unjustified advantage of the daily press by promoting Sunday advertising? If a newspaper published a special Sunday edition, it would be promptly prosecuted. I understand that by the radio corporation's activities some $200,000 worth of newspaper and periodical advertising has been seriously affected. Has it been considered what effect this will have on labour, on employment?
Occasional features which have been introduced by the broadcasting corporation are satisfactory; but where does the $1,500,000

revenue from licence fees go? And where will the extra 3750,000 go?-and it may be 31,500,000 extra, when one takes into account the taxing of duplicate sets.
The reception is no better for the vast majority of listeners, and the programs are no better than they were.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the money obtained in licence fees should go for the improvement of Canadian programs and Canadian information, and if necessary Canadian advertising, and to help develop Canadian talent-that is, if the licence fee is to be collected at all.
Our democracy has not failed, but it is not functioning properly. Corruption must be eliminated, or democracy will fail. I cannot let this opportunity pass without drawing attention to the danger. The democratic countries of the world to-day are the only countries in which freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of religion and personal liberty remain.
We in Canada have the privilege of living in a democracy, but if we are to continue to enjoy -that privilege the people of this country must realize the obligations they have in return for that privilege.
The man who comes in smiling like a Cheshire cat on election day, after voting, and says, "Well, I have done my duty," has only exercised his privilege; but has he realized the obligation he has for the privileges he enjoys under our democracy? We are supposed to have government of the people, for the people, by the people.
One of the troubles to-day is the apathy of the public with respect to current politics in this country. People say: I don't take part in politics because it is such a dirty game. If this be true, who let it get that way? Apathy on the part of the public-no realization of their obligations. We have a great many problems which are more or less taken for granted by the public and are very little understood, but which we are told are to be solved by governments.
The public must take an active interest in politics, without remuneration, not for the sake of patronage, -but in defence of democratic principles, as a part of their obligations, if democracy is to survive.
What are governments for? Lord Baldwin has said that the consensus of opinion is that governments are for the attainment by the people of the highest degree of wellbeing and virtue.
How many people realize that for every dollar they spend in Canada they get less than sixty cents value, the balance being taken in taxes in some form or other? When

The Address-Mr. Pelletier
governments pay, it all comes out of the pockets of the people, either in taxes or in reduced wages. Why is it that people who are generally thrifty in the management of their own domestic affairs, when it comes to public matters seem to think that governments are Christmas trees for money to be picked from?
Governments are always influenced by votes, and votes come from people with varying degrees of intelligence. Some say that the franchise is too wide. Be that as it may, it is a fact, not a theory, and we cannot alter it. It is therefore necessary for those with a certain degree of intelligence to inform and influence those who are not so intelligent, and in turn to be influenced by those with greater intelligence. Votes should not be influenced in any way except by reason, if democracy is to survive. It is the public's obligation to inform themselves accurately upon the various aspects of the problems coming before them; in other words, to take an intelligent interest in public life. It is the duty of members of parliament, and of the press, to inform their public accurately and truthfully. If one reads the history of the decline of the Athenian democracy, one must realize that it was brought about by just the same conditions as exist today,-patronage, apathy, and leave-it-to-George. In the words of the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, now Lord Baldiwn of Bewdley:
The Greeks talked incessantly of equalities and butchered each other for it;
We are not quite as bad as that yet.
... of freedom, and lived on the labour of slaves. Freedom of speech was stifled and public men who refused to advocate pleasures for the multitude were banished. Politicians rivalled one another in bribing the electorate. There was an unemployment problem and a policy of public works, payment to jurymen, free seats at the theatres. Those who had triumphed over tyrants in turn became despotic. Those who had been oppressed became in turn oppressors. Those who had denounced luxury and idleness in individuals succumbed to the temptations of riches when shared out by the state and by and by Plutarch records that the Athenians from being a sober and thrifty and self supporting people, turned into lovers of expense, intemperance and license.
The attitude in this country taken by some institutions and businesses in frowning on the activities of their employees in politics for fear of the effect it might have with respect to themselves on the party in power, the unconscious coercion they feel, is to say the least bad for democracy; it is not democracy functioning. Our democracy is worth fighting for. The peace of the world is not attacked by democracy. Another of the difficulties
encountered in attempting a solution of our problems is the lack of confidence and the suspicion existing between institutions, labour, industry and departments of government. I am sure that a closer cooperation and frankness is necessary for a better feeling of security throughout the country. I plead that every effort be put forth to preserve our democracy and make Canada the best place in the world in which to live. A real effort is necessary and a lot of hard work and effort by us all.
I support the amendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It was not my intention to participate in this debate, but having listened to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) I felt I could not remain silent, in .the face of the charges he has brought into this house. The words of the hon. gentleman indicate that there has come into his possession evidence of irregularities and corruption in the matter of government contracts. He contended that certain amounts of money were being levied on contractors. He said that he could produce evidence in so far as Canadian National Railway contracts were concerned. Apparently many people in this country are being compelled by means of such levies to contribute to funds for political purposes, resulting in corrupt practices.
Today I directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and I regret to say that I cannot believe the answer is satisfactory to members of this house. It seems to me that there are other ways and means of getting at the truth of this matter than those enumerated by the leader of the government, and I suggest to him that a committee of this house should be instructed to investigate the matter. It is not necessary to appoint a new committee. Under the rules of the house we have a standing committee on privileges and elections, and a reference by the government to that committee would compel the leader of the opposition to make good the charges he has made in this house. In my belief it is absolutely necessary that we should do that. If the matter is allowed to remain in its present position a stigma will be left on this house, a stigma that should be removed, and I feel sure that all hon. members will join me in demanding that a proper investigation of these charges be made.
So far as we in the province of Alberta are concerned, our people pay for our election; they elect us themselves, and we are responsible to them. We were under the impression that the old ward politicians' tactics of the past had more or less disappeared. It seems to
The Address-Mr. Pelletier

me we have no other course than to see that these charges are thoroughly investigated. We do not believe for one moment that any leader of a political party in this country would knowingly permit such a thing to go on; rather it is done by supporters of political parties without the knowledge of the leaders of those parties, and undoubtedly it will be the desire of the leaders concerned to have this matter threshed out. I noticed that when, the other day, the charges were made by the leader of the opposition, hon. members, and particularly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) were quick to resent the accusations. It was said that Canadian National Railway contracts had been tampered with. The Minister of Transport would certainly be the first to wish to know whether such things have been going on. I do not believe any cabinet minister, past or present, would knowingly permit such practices; therefore the matter should certainly be looked into.
I might add that our young people can have no faith in our institutions if matters of this kind are to be hushed up and passed over. It is our duty to act in such a way as to build up their faith in our institutions. Is it possible to do so if, knowing that a member of this house is in possession of documents which prove political or electoral corruption, we allow those documents to remain unseen and unknown? It is quite true that it is possible for an individual to put up a deposit of a thousand dollars or some such sum in order to have charges of corruption brought before the proper authority. It seems to me that, of all people in this country, the man who made the charges is best able to produce the thousand dollars. But whether that is so or not, there is no reason why the thing should be done in that manner. The house possesses the necessary facilities to investigate this matter, and in my opinion an investigation should be made.
There will be an occasion later on, I am sure, to touch upon the various subjects mentioned in the speech from the throne. When those subjects are brought down will be the time, in my opinion, to express approval or disapproval of what the measures contemplate. My sole purpose in rising is to say that if we remain silent with respect to the charges to which I have alluded we shall be guilty of connivance in regard to the things which are said to have taken place. I do not believe it is the desire of any hon. member that such a condition should prevail.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this debate, and I am simply filling in on behalf of the 
opposition. I wish to say a few words, as representing the man on the street, to the man in the cabinet. I looked over the speech from the throne and I am very much disappointed that nothing more satisfactory has been presented to parliament, at a time when we have so many roving commissions, travelling like minstrel shows all over Canada. Provided they could sing a bit and blacken their faces they would be more successful as minstrels than they are as political commissions, which get nowhere and are appointed for no other reason than to postpone action by the government of the day on questions with which they will not deal.
I realize that it is the function and duty of the opposition often to criticize the government of the day. We as an opposition are disappointed. I realize that the cabinet consists of some very able men, and that we have a government of Canadians. But realizing this I regret to say that in the speech from the throne the man on the street, the large number of people on relief, and the municipalities that are finding the burden of taxation on real estate becoming intolerable, are very much disappointed that something of a practical nature has not been done. In this country with its vast resources, if we solved the problem of distribution, there should be no one starving. But there is not a word in the speech from the throne about this great problem of distribution. In fact I am surprised that the speech from the throne was not delivered in the debating society of the university of Toronto or the mock parliament at McGill.
In passing I wish to congratulate the Commonwealth of Australia on its 150th anniversary. I should like to see a delegation from Canada visit our sister dominion on this occasion. They have decided that Australia for all time shall be a white man's country. They do not believe in separatism. They realize that an armed Britain is the greatest defence of the peace of the world, that Britain stands as trustee for the peace of the civilized world.
Lord Milner once said that money-bags are proverbially short-sighted. Our moneybags were short-sighted when they called for the appointment of the Rowell commission. I have a high regard for Chief Justice Rowell. I believe if he were a one-man commission the results would be better. But I do not believe in these commissions at all. It seems that this government believes that a commission a day keeps the unemployed away; that appears to be the principle on which all these

The Address-Mr. Church
roving commissions are appointed. The members of this parliament might as well all go home; owing to these commissions we have no powers, we cannot force anything to a vote. Our powers are taken away and handed over to the house of Rowell and Dafoe, of whom the latter, from what I have known of him as a free trader and his stand on the grain trade and other matters has been one of the chief foes, on some questions of the prairie provinces. Last session and the session before I brought to the attention of the house my submission that constitutional and parliamentary and law reform was one of the most important matters before parliament. The government said they were going to appoint a commission. 1 wish to take issue with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in regard to his statement that the chairman of that commission is a judicial officer. That point was raised in the Gamey-Stratton case. Sitting in the city halLjn Toronto were Chancellor Boyd and Chief Justice Falconbridge, and it was decided that as members of that commission those gentlemen were no longer judges, they were not entitled to the title given them in the law courts, they were just commissioners, and were called Mr. Chairman or Mr. Commissioner.
There are too many of these judges leaving the bench. Hon. members will remember the customs scandal some years ago when three judges, Mr. Justice Roy of Quebec, Mr. Justice Brown of Regina and Mr. Justice Wright of Toronto went up and down this country for a year and nine months, leaving their judicial duties. The work of the courts in Ontario is becoming congested today; several judges have died and others are out on these roving commissions.
The time has come when parliament should regain its powers. I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in what he said about this matter, that the government of the day, with so many Liberal governments in power in the provinces, should have settled these matters sitting around a table with them. I do not agree with what has been said in .praise of the work of the fathers of confederation in the British North America Act, far from it. I believe they were the most short-sighted body of .men that ever got together in a room at any time anywhere. Look at the resulting provincial situation. There never should have been any provincial legislatures. I wish to speak of the fathers of confederation with respect, but when we see the way they launched these provincial legislatures on the country it is difficult to admire them. They do not have all these
governments in Great Britain. The result of having them here is that we have overtaxation and overgovernment. We have 10,000,000 people; Great Britain has 47,000,000, but they get along with one government there. They did not have state legislatures in Australia until recently. The confederation act should be recast. That is what I understood this Rowell commission was appointed for, but now we find that it is a roving omnibus commission on everything. I noticed the members of the commission around Ottawa for some time and now I read that they have gone east. But wise men come from the east. The star of this commission is in its decline. The municipalities have simply been humbugged in submitting briefs to it. The commission had the former German chancellor here to advise them, probably Gandhi will be the next witness called by them.
Royal commissions are a favourite resort of the present federal government for postponing action when action is imperatively required. Take the burden of taxation on real estate; are we to wait three or four years before getting relief from that? There is the prison commission, the textile commission. the commission about automobiles, the tariff commission; it seems to go around in a circle, but no relief comes to the unemployed. Now it is proposed we should have a new flag. Let us get rid of the black flag first. The unemployed and the farmers on relief do not want reports of a commission when they see the black flag flying in front of their houses and are put out on the street; they have the facts. So have the returned men who fought for men in and out of this house. This commission will achieve nothing. I had a big pile of books that I threw away the other day, reports of various commissions made since I have been a member of the house. They will achieve nothing-that is why they are appointed- except a boost from the corporation press. They are only advisory in any event, and as soon as the advice is given it will be discarded and the report pigeonholed. The Prime Minister said they were appointed to get the facts, but they will find out nothing that the country does not know already. They may well be described as a minstrel troupe. Some of the briefs that have been handed in are made up from pamphlets and booklets and government reports as old as this country. They are a commission in a Pickwickian sense-with apologies to Pickwick.
In all common sense, if we view the situation, everything depends upon the instructions which have been given by the government of the day. The personnel of these
The Address-Mr. Church

commissions has been chosen for political purposes and political expediency; the interests of the people are being overlooked, just at a time when action is needed on many important matters. For instance, to-morrow a deputation of mayors is coming to Ottawa to interview the government.
Ten years ago the leader of the Progressive party and I proposed that one-third of the cost of relief should be borne by the dominion, one-third by the province and one-third by the municipality. That system was tried out and found to be practical. I think we were right then; I still think so. As my leader has said, if the Liberal premiers had sat around a table for stocktaking they would have obtained far better results. Sickness and unemployment insurance was part of the Liberal platform of 1921. If there had been a round table conference that question could have been dealt with satisfactorily, instead of having these commissions act according to the expediency of the moment.
In England today, Mr. Speaker, they have a radical government, although it is called Conservative. They have had a survey made and they are going to nationalize the coal mines. Not very long ago we appointed the Tory commission to investigate our coal question. The chairman, I always thought, was Tory in name only, and I was sure of that when I read his report, which deals with everything except the spread in price from S5.25 a ton in 1905 to $14.50 last year. The report says nothing about a national coal supply. With the cold weather we have in Canada and the way our resources are being squandered the next generation is going to face a scarcity of coal. Conservation is one of the most important things in this country. I should like to see not a report issued by a royal commission but a survey made by the government towards the end of nationalizing the coal mines of this country. It is only during the last seventy-five years that science has discovered the power inherent in coal, oil and falling water. We have nationalized the falling water, from which we obtain light, power and transportation. This country is the richest in the world in power, possessing 42,000,000 horse-power, of which only one-sixth or 7,000,000 horse-power have been developed. The water supply in our municipalities has been nationalized, but that is as far as we have gone. When I first came into the house I suggested that our oil should be nationalized so that a pipe line might bring Alberta oil to the people of the country. The nationalization of the coal mines in [Mr. Church.)
England, which is expected to be consummated by the summer of 1942, will cost the mother country $332,250,000. The commission we appointed, with all its experts, did nothing.
Back in 1922 and 1923, when I proposed a national coal policy for this country so that the fuel consumed in Canada would be mined under the British flag, whether in Wales or Alberta or the maritime provinces, I was laughed at. I proposed a system of bonuses, subventions and subsidies. There was laughter and ridicule in the house, but at last that suggestion was adopted, and today two million tons of coal are being moved economically from the maritime provinces to the head of the lakes. We can thank the leader of the opposition for supporting that nolic3r and putting it into practical effect. Now I want to see a report made along the lines I have suggested.
I do not see the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) in the house. A few years ago I called his attention to the question of income tax. After it was discovered in Washington that Mr. Pierpont Morgan, the Van Sweringens of Cleveland, and other wealthy people paid no income tax, I asked the minister if he would not consider having an inquiry into the matter of income tax here, but he never even answered my question. Now, if you ask me, again he has been weighed in the balance and found wanting as a minister in his treatment of customs matters in Toronto. Over the protests of the mayor, the city council, the board of trade and other civic bodies, and over the heads of government supporters from Toronto, his department has gone to work and divided the port of Toronto, causing great chaos in that city. I believe it is the duty of a minister of the crown to consult local people in connection with a public utility of this kind. I am not saying anything about the ability of the minister, far from it. I have no personal quarrel with him. I believe he has a hard department to handle, but I was sorry to see him take that action without consulting the people interested.
On more than one occasion, Mr. Speaker, I have introduced a bill with regard to newspapers. I am surprised at the way this parliament is treated by the Canadian press. Turn to any of our leading newspapers and you will find four or five pages about some prize fighter; there will be great ballyhoo about professional athletes of all kinds, but you will see only about a column or so devoted to the House of Commons and the problems that concern this country. I am

The Address-Mr. Church
afraid the press of Canada are following the press of England. The only independent newspaper they had over there that would speak out for the empire was the Morning Post, and now it has lost its identity, having been sold to the Telegraph. I am free to admit, as I said in speaking to my newspaper bill, that in peace and war alike the press do fine work, but in the present condition of affairs in Canada I believe it is the duty of the press to support the government when right as far as possible and do what they can to educate the people in connection with public affairs. I think that is a duty the newspapers owe to the people of this country, in these days of stress through which we are passing.
I have referred to the question of direct relief and the high tax rate that it has brought about. To-day no one wants to own real estate. Millions of dollars of additional taxes for relief have been placed on Toronto real estate, and I do not know how the people are going to carry on. Of the Toronto tax rate four or five mills are devoted to the care of the unemployed, the ill and the suffering, although a federal burden. Speaking of the sick, parliament spends about three and a half million dollars on the health of animals, but what about human health? We have had epidemics of infantile paralysis; we have many other diseases that are widespread; yet all we spend on public health is $442,000 out of $600,000,000. The other day we read in the press about a poor woman in Nova Scotia who was very ill during childbirth. A doctor tried to reach her but, through no fault of his own, was unable to save her life. When we read such things in the newspapers, and see the very high death rate from different diseases we should realize that the time has come when, instead of having a national skeleton health department, we should have one that will be adequate to take care of this most important work. I hope parliament will take a forward step in this connection.
I hope the Department of Labour will bring forward within the very near future some plan which will provide index figures for families with incomes under $1,200, with the cost of food, rent and other expenses. The minister is continually tinkering with his relief bill, so that the municipalities do not know where they stand. I am asking for a stable policy. The people do not want relief; they want work.
There has been mention of the government's policy of defence. I hope that some day in Canada we may have a generation of Canadians who will think far enough ahead to save Canada by careful preparation rather
than by wasteful and bloody sacrifice such as we have known before. In its defence policy the present government has done everything by fits and starts, and has done nothing right. An armed Britain is the greatest security we can have for the peace of the world. We are not dependent upon the Monroe doctrine or upon a pan-American doctrine. If we were we would have cause to be sorry some day.
We must depend upon an armed Britain because we have practically no air force, no fleet and only a very small armament. In many ways Canada is in grave danger to-day. On the other hand many of the proposed expenditures are wasteful. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) is not in his seat, but speaking at the St. Henry by-election on January 12, he said, according to reports in the Quebec and Ontario press:
Our outlay for armaments is only seven per cent of our national budget, a modest expenditure. Some of our cannons are very venerable; much of our artillery is still drawn by horses. We must modernize, and that is just what we are doing.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) proposed to complete the building of the Canadian National station. Further, he agreed to take away level crossings. I do not blame him for making those promises, when speaking in a by-election contest. At the same time, speaking as the acting-Minister of Public Works to-day, he should have realized that from Niagara-on-the-Lake to Queenston and Lewiston and lake Erie to Chippawa the Niagara river is a navigable stream, and it is the duty of the government to have ice-breakers to keep it in proper condition. The ice could have been regulated, just as it is regulated on the St. Lawrence river. However, I sometimes think the minister does not want to do anything for Ontario. It is all right to spend huge sums, millions of dollars, for development in the Richelieu river canal, but when it comes to protecting power companies on the Niagara river in Ontario, which are owned by the municipalities or by the province, from this great danger, he has not a cent to offer.
In my view one of the results of the rise of dictatorships has been the silencing of pacifists the world over. If any people could be held responsible for bringing the British Empire almost to the verge of destruction, they are the ones. However for the last while we have not heard much from them. I hope some steps may now be taken to tell the country something about Canada's defence policy. What is Canada's defence policy? Does anybody know what it is? No, nobody knows. I have been trying to find out what
The Address-Mr. Church

member of the government is in charge of Canada's external affairs and foreign policy. The present government appears to object to the constitutional, traditional principle whereby all questions of Canada's foreign policy and the administration of its external affairs and of this great trust must be put before the House of Commons by the government in power. Will we have opportunity to challenge some of the actions of our government?
It is all very well to be dependent upon the United States, but may I point out that in the August, 1937, issue of the English Review there has been a criticism of that policy:
We have recently seen a great push in favour of the American trade agreement. " What is our trade with the dominions compared to what our trade with the United States might be?" is the slogan, and we are adjured in many quarters to drop the substance of preference for' the shadow of American goodwill. It is just as well for us to remember the occasions since the war when we have altered our policy in the hope of pleasing Americans of the United States. The first of these was the establishment of the league of nations as part of the Treaty of Versailles. We agreed to this at the behest of President Wilson; France only consented on condition that Great Britain and the United States of America gave her a joint guarantee of security. The ink was hardly dry upon the parchments when the United States of America refused to honour President Wilson's signature, and alike repudiated the Versailles Treaty, the guarantee of security, and the league of nations. The next great change in our policy "to please the Americans" was at Washington in 1922, when we abandoned our alliance with the Japanese, who had been our invaluable and faithful allies for nearly twenty years. The result is the loss of Japanese support and friendship, but no gain in America of either. One more notable instance of the pursuit of American goodwill and failure to attain it was seen in the Irish Treaty. We were told by the promoters of this affair that "if only we would give way in Ireland" to the gunmen who had been murdering the British "the last resentment of America against us would die away." We gave way to the gunmen. Ireland is more embittered than ever and the United States of America just as unfriendly. This new proposal comes from a set of people who will join with any project likely to damage this country. In this case the motive force is Gold. America buys gold, South Africa produces large quantities yearly, Canada and Russia are also gold producers. The power behind the movement to get us into an American treaty is the power of the gold producers, backed by the gold manipulators of the world. They want us to buy American goods in order that she may buy their gold.
That is from a leading review in England, and is written by a great man.

With respect to the Anglo-American pact may I say that, I am not one of those Conservatives who on all occasions wishes to apologize for this party's action in defeating reciprocity in 1911. Reciprocity in those days would have made a Lazarus out of every man in Canada, and of a country that Laurier had said he made a nation, just as it would have made a Lazarus out of every returned man who fought at Amiens, Vimy Ridge or any other field of Canadian glory.
I am not in favour of handing over our own market to the Americans or to any other people. I believe in the policy of Joseph Chamberlain, that great man who introduced in 1906 the policy of imperial preference. Had those policies been carried out thirty years ago we would not have had the war which broke out in 1914.
The British trade agreement was ably secured by the present leader of the opposition in 1932, which gives him the leading place in history. By bringing about the Ottawa agreements the present leader of the opposition in that year made the dream of Joseph Chamberlain come true. What did the present Prime Minister in England have to say about it at the Conservative convention there. He said that as a result of that treaty the trade from the dominions to the motherland had increased by 41 per cent, and the trade from the motherland to the dominions had increased by 46 per cent. There had been a corresponding increase in international trade. That was the result of the treaty which was made by my right hon. leader, and which was thus twice blest. Are we going to give up the advantages we gained from it over to the United States? Certainly we are not going to give it up for something that is uncertain.
The Anglo-American treaty is not commercial. Rather it is a political treaty brought forward in an effort to gain support for the government. A very fine gesture has been made by President Roosevelt. It was a gesture to try to get out of the supreme court difficulty. It is well known that he is in wrong with the cotton growers of the south and the farmers of the middle west, with respect to his new deal policy. It will be just a political treaty and will last only three years as the Republicans have announced that they will abrogate it if they are returned to power. Australia and New Zealand are looking at this proposed treaty with a great deal of doubt.

The Address-Mr. Church
When I look at the counters in the departmental stores in Toronto I can see why our home market is ruined with goods there from foreign countries. Canada is being made a dumping ground for cheap and shoddy goods from about thirty countries of the world to the loss of our steady home market. The result is that no home market exists. I stand where I stood thirty years ago on the Conservative platform, our own work for our own workmen and our own markets for our own products. That is as true today as it was then.
This Anglo-American treaty is not a commercial treaty; it is political in all its aspects. We should make every effort to see that its terms are not carried out. Are we going to make a similar mistake and enter into the same sort of haphazard treaty? Are we going to enter into a treaty which will do more harm than good? If we do we will soon see the mistake we have made on the war debt policy. Canada is a commercial country; England is a commercial country, and the British Empire is a commercial empire. Our problems are commercial and it is the duty of our statesmen to draw closer the commercial ties between the various parts of the empire. That is what our statesmen should be doing instead of giving away their markets to the United States or clamouring over the strife in Europe.
This government must decide its attitude toward industry. Is industry in this country to be fettered and bound? Industry should be run by those who understand it, not by a lot of amateurs and university professors who sit on the different commissions. I object to too much interference by the state in the conduct of business. At the same time, I believe that labour should be given a larger share of the profits and rewards of industry.
To go back to this Anglo-American treaty. The senate of the United States may take away from the president the power he possesses now to make these agreements.
I am glad the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is in the chamber as I have something I should like to draw to his attention. I am much concerned over the great loss of life in motor accidents. A committee of the House of Lords was appointed to look into this question and after it had made its report it was found that the number of accidents in Great Britain decreased considerably. The time has come when we should make an effort to stop this loss of life. A committee of this house should be appointed to inquire
into this matter. If we were to put up wooden crosses for those who have lost their lives and those who have been injured in Canada during the past five years we would not have room to place them outside the parliament buildings even though they were put only two inches apart.
The time has come when the people of this country expect results from the party system. Unless we get busy, no one knows what will happen in 1940. I have been told by some that there will be an election this year, while others have said there will not. Who will win then? That reminds me of the battle of Dundee where some said, "we ran," others said, "they ran" and others said, "nobody ran." Unless the government get busy they will hear from the working people of this country.
The British dominions are being threatened by this proposed agreement. This Anglo-American treaty is more political than commercial. It is one of the results of the European situation and the race in rearming. We have lost two of our best allies in Italy and Japan and this is one of the results of our diplomatic reverses. This gesture is being made toward the United States as the result of the foreign policy of Great Britain. For generations the policy has been that trade should follow the flag, but that seems to have been thrown overboard. This treaty will destroy empire preference and empire cooperation and union. We are taking a backward step in the matter of preference from the steps taken in the days of Joseph Chamberlain, Sir John Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. This is a heading that appeared in the Washington Post of November 17, 1937:
Trade Treaty Between U.S. and Britain is Imminent
Call to Negotiations Due Momentarily in Reply to Fascist Moves Political Meaning to Rival Economic
This agreement will destroy the structure of the Ottawa agreements. It means a breaking of faith with India and the other members of the empire.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, upon perusing very carefully the speech from the throne the one thing that struck me was its vagueness. It would appear that the Liberal party, now that they have attained power, have lost many of those fine qualities of which they spoke so glibly in their days of opposition. I have made a point in the last few days of going through some old Hansards, and I find that in the Liberal party there are
The Address-Mr. Poole

many extremists; but that was when they were in opposition. That was when they were appealing to the electorate. But not now- that is all forgotten.
The question of trade has been dealt with, and some indication given of new agreements to be made. It was said in this house the other day, or at least implied, that the social credit people do not value trade. Let me say here and now that we have never minimized the value of trade. We recognize its value, but we also recognize the unnatural restrictions on trade because of the shortage of purchasing power in the hands of consumers in every part of the world. We do not, however, look upon trade as a solution of our economic ills. We do not believe that a market in Japan for Canadian goods is of greater value than a market in Canada. It is our belief that the people of Canada should be fed first, that they should have access to the goods that can be produced in such abundance in this country.
Living conditions in this country have not improved since this government came into power to the extent they would have us believe by their jubilant speeches made across this country in the recent by-elections. We would probably have more sympathy with the government if it was through their efforts that trade had been increased, and if commodities which have been	sold in	greatervolume had been natural commodities, commodities that	were going	to add	to	thehappiness and	health and	wealth	of	thepeoples of the world. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that the goods which have been shipped out of this country, and which are responsible for the slight	increase in	production	and
some semblance of prosperity, have been metals to be used for armament purposes. I think it is a terrible price for the Canadian consumer to pay, in order that he may have a job to-day and perhaps one to-morrow, that we should better our conditions by supplying Japan with war materials which to-morrow may be used to shoot down and destroy Canadian youth. If that is the only kind of trade we can depend upon, if that is the only way we can have brief prosperity, then I say the price is too great.
There is one subject I want to discuss in the short time at my disposal, and that is the attitude of this government with regard to the province of Alberta. What we have endeavoured and are endeavouring to accomplish there at the present time is exactly what was advocated by the present Prime Minister when he was appealing to the electorate in 1935-to issue credit in terms of

public need. The difference, however, is that we meant what we said but the Prime Minister did not, or probably the Prime Minister did not have the same public in mind. I know that the people of western Canada, and I have travelled over it extensively in the past year, have not been the beneficiaries of any new financial policy. I have seen no credit in their hands. The only credit they have is real credit; that is, the ability to work, the ability to construct; but they have never had the opportunity of applying that all-important financial credit to their real credit in order that they may enjoy the wealth of the Dominion of Canada.
The province of Alberta brought down to the legislature three measures that were passed by the house but were disallowed by this government. I wonder what this Liberal government is going to do about the padlock law of Quebec. Is there one rule for the west and another for the east? Is Quebec privileged? The difference, Mr. Speaker, is that the padlock law was going to close up and destroy those organizations which had banded themselves together for the express purpose of making their way out of their terrible conditions.
It struck me as rather strange the other day when I read in the press of a minister speaking in Quebec about communism. Last year I attended a public meeting in this city where again they expressed their horror of communism. I fear communism far less than I fear the laissez-faire policies of the Liberal government, because communism is the cause of nothing; it is an effect. I am not defending it. I am not a communist, but I believe that in a democracy every section of society has the right to express its opinion and the right to enjoy the same privileges as anybody else. They have the right to be wrong. I look upon the padlock law of Quebec as the first step towards a fascist state. There has been no effort made on the part of this government to disallow that law, but it moved with great rapidity to disallow the Alberta legislation. Of course, the difference was that the measures we proposed were against that all-powerful organization, the money organization.
May I, Mr. Speaker, ask the Liberal government to give us at least some indication of when they are going to bring down some measure of monetary reform and tell us when they are going to issue credit in terms of public need? We still have thousands of unemployed people in this country; we still have thousands of our fellow-citizens living under deplorable conditions while at the same

The Address-Mr. Poole
time we have available all kinds of building material, all kinds of human labour and all kinds of machines, and at a time when, there is no question about the need for better conditions. Unfortunately the Liberal government has not yet issued credit in terms of public need. I say again this year, as I did last year, that if you are depending upon trade agreements and expanding markets to bring about prosperity, God help the people of Canada. I question the sincerity of the Liberal government. When I saw the Prime Minister come into this chamber on the first day leading with pride the new Liberal members, I thought it might have been more appropriate if the leader of the opposition had led them in, because I have always contended that the present leader of the opposition was the leader of the Liberal party, since it was through his failures that they got where they are. On the other hand it is just as true,
I think that the Prime Minister is the leader of the Conservative party, because it is through the failures of this government that the Conservative party will go back again.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The other day the leader of the opposition, turning in the direction of the Prime Minister, said something to this effect, "I do not see any great difference between your policy and the policy which I pursued." I agree. The only difference between them is the height of the tariff wall. They have never yet dealt with a real issue; and if this speech from the throne is any indication of their activities this coming year, the Canadian people can expect no great measure of reform from the Liberal government.
At the beginning of my address I said that in the Liberal party there were extremists. I find in Hansard of February 1, 1934, at a time when the Liberal party sat to the left of the Speaker, the following extract from one of the platform addresses of Mr. J. A. MacMillan:
I am not an extremist, but I believe that the same authority that came into our homes during the war and took our sons from the knees of their mothers, because there was a national emergency, should not be afraid to take similar steps to bring to the aid of the nation all surplus wealth. We conscripted men, why not money? There is now another national emergency that will have to be faced resolutely and squarely, if the country is to weather the storm. One of the ways out of the difficulty would be to get rid of the terrible burden of interest by paying off a substantial portion of the national debt, and this can only be done by conscription of wealth.
The speaker was not a social crediter or a member representing the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation; he was a Liberal who now sits on the government benches. What has happened since that platform address was delivered? Just one thing. The Liberals have come into power, and now, I suggest, they are afraid to tackle this problem, afraid to deal with the cause of depression. That cause is definitely money, purchasing power. There is no such thing as a depression. A "depression" would suggest that we are short of goods. If we were short of goods there would be no unemployed. We have plenty of goods; we have also plenty of people who cannot get the goods; and the only purpose of our productive machine, our whole economic machine, is to enrich life by making available to the people all those things that can be produced by the knowledge of men.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
